fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Spanish Teacher and the Three Percent Idea", "body": "Hess traces her twenty some years in flower remedies to a stretch abroad after college, where she studied herbalism, essential oils and acupuncture before meeting a flower remedy expert from Spain who taught only in Spanish, and only in Spain, Mexico and Argentina. She says he left her with two ideas: that every botanical, tree and growing thing carries a specific emotional, mental or energetic benefit, and that if three percent of the world's population worked with these remedies, the ripple effect would change the future of the planet. She brought the work back to the United States in 2001, when, as she puts it, yoga was not yet cool."}, {"title": "Doctrine of Signatures and the Language of Flowers", "body": "Chance opens on the Doctrine of Signatures, the principle that how a plant looks, smells and grows is key to understanding its virtues, and Hess extends the idea past Victorian flower symbolism. She describes a 4.5 billion year old living earth in which each flower is a thread of wisdom, an antenna transmitting information, and claims a person absorbs some of it just by being around it. Their dandelion exchange is the case in point. Hess reads the children's rhyme about flicking the flower head off as folk memory of the plant's signature, while Chance offers a world tree cosmology where every plant is one branch of a single organism."}, {"title": "Scaling Dew: How the Elixirs Get Made", "body": "Asked how the elixirs are made, Hess describes a practice she says turns up in Africa, Australia, the Himalayas, Europe and Central America, most commonly as drinking the dew drops from the tops of flowers, or having a healer soak chosen blooms in sunlit water and pour it over your head. LOTUSWEI, she says, has simply figured out how to scale dew and get it into a bottle, since Phoenix is far too dry for the real thing. Flowers are used because the flower holds the most energy in a plant as its reproductive part, sunlight is the catalyst that drives the life force into water, and alcohol stabilizes it."}, {"title": "Water as Recording Device, Body as Screen", "body": "Hess maintains there are no chemical constituents at work, only what she calls the chi or life force, and compares water to a recording device, reaching for DVDs, cassette tapes and cell phones as things we use without understanding. She cites UK research she says found bees are drawn to flowers by a subtle electrical frequency felt through the hairs on their legs rather than by color or scent. Her clearest framing is death: the 21 grams that leave the body, she says, is the layer flower essences work on, with the body as a screen and consciousness as the projector, an image Chance ties to his biofield tuning work."}, {"title": "Static, Blind Spots and the Flower Revolution", "body": "Both describe a world that has grown noisier. Chance frames ambient EMF, refrigerator hum and urban smells as things we constantly filter out, each one a drain on the battery of our awareness, and Hess says her own practice has changed over two decades, while admitting she cannot say whether EMFs, toxicity or human evolution explain it. She calls the essences one of the gentlest ways to surface blind spots, and points listeners to the Flower Revolution subscription, where roughly 150 members receive the same new elixir monthly and compare notes, the flower picking quiz on lotuswei.com, and her Self Rising Nature Center in Phoenix."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Katie Hess of LotusWei joins InnerVerse to share the incredible healing power of flowers! We discuss how she found her plant essence path, the language of flowers, the Radiant Energy Elixir, and others, the history and science of flower essences, how subtle energy medicines transform your world from the inside out, throat chakra dynamics, and the curative quality of epiphany.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, Katie shares about her book Flowerevolution, how flowers represent and support us through transitions into the unknown, the meditative aspect of tactical training, the similarities between warriors and healers, magical places of the world and their rare flowers, the exponential factor of homeopathic preparations, astrology & the doctrine of signatures, and creative DIY ways to work with plants.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Transitions as Doorways Into the Unknown", "body": "Katie frames the biggest thresholds of life, from giving birth to the moment of death to a career path ending, as leaps into the unknown, and notes how often women tell her they are afraid of success, projecting abandonment or loss onto the very thing they want. The conversation turns to the belief that good fortune invites the other shoe to drop, a pattern the two dub the Job complex. Katie's answer is learning to hold space for ourselves no matter what arises, with flower essences widening the gap between a trigger and an old reaction."}, {"title": "Static Culture Versus a Nature of Change", "body": "Chance describes a culture of static that tells people to stay put and run the same hamster wheel, calling it the most antithetical philosophy to nature, where the only constant is change and you are either growing or decaying. Katie adds that we divorce ourselves from feelings we judge as bad, like anger or betrayal, which only grips them tighter, and suggests offering ourselves the same understanding we would give a best friend. Chance closes the thread with a paradox: accepting other people's hard feelings, rather than rejecting them, is what keeps you protected."}, {"title": "Tactical Training as a Meditation Practice", "body": "Asked what she rarely discusses, Katie reveals she took up firearms training in 2021, committing to six months of Saturday sessions with a group of ten. At the range she watches her breath and whether any part of her is bracing for the boom, and realized the trigger pull resembles the moment of death, a choice nobody else can make for her. She describes ice bucket drills and shrinking targets, a class of twenty she hosted in Phoenix that turned out to be all healers, intuitives and doctors, and her surprise that the hardest part was using her voice to say back off."}, {"title": "The Warrior and the Healer as One Coin", "body": "Chance offers the saying that it is better to be a warrior in a garden than a gardener in a war, arguing that healing needs boundaries and that the warrior holds the line, like an archer on the rampart deciding which thoughts may cross the gate. He ties the decisive moment of taking the shot to creativity, noting that warrior monks were also painters and poets. Katie describes her twelve year old niece becoming the best shooter in the group, and her own growing interest in opting out, standing firm, and harnessing our sense of wild."}, {"title": "Rare Flowers, Living Plants, and Signatures", "body": "Katie finds that each region carries a theme, with Costa Rican orchids dissolving buried fears, Iceland evoking childlike wonder and Southeast Asia radiating abundance. After three months of daily prayer she found an endangered white fringed orchid in Minnesota within ten minutes, as thunder rolled from a single wispy cloud. She explains that one mother essence can serve generations, contrasted with forty roses for a drop of oil, and describes charting an essence's collection date astrologically, reading the doctrine of signatures, soaking blossoms in sunlight or moonlight, and simply asking a plant for help."}]
